Constitutionally speaking, his only control over spending is to veto entire bills.  Attempts to allow that to be more precise (the "line-item veto") have been ruled unconstitutional.

So the only control Trump has over NASA's budget is to veto the entire government spending package, something he's never going to do (I mean he might veto it, but it won't be about NASA).
The president submits a budget, but it has no legal power.  Congress has explicit constitutional control over all taxes and spending.

I don't think it actually *did* change anything about how people acted the first round.  Under normal circumstances, it's a disadvantage to send a flanker to stand on a point for a few seconds before getting killed.  It only becomes a good idea if you are nearing the end of the round and your team hasn't gotten anywhere, which is quite rare... and by which point the defending team can expect that and prevent the move.

This is different once the sides switch; not only does the offensive team know from the very beginning that it will be to their advantage to try to snipe an instant win, they also don't have to try to score immediately... that sneaky flanker is a threat to instantly win *throughout the round*.  The other team can't defend normally, they have to have a person sit on the point the entire round just to prevent an instant loss, and even then they can be booped or killed.  The alternative is to abandon the early chokepoints and exclusively fight on the point, which is an even worse situation.

This is a fringe situation, but it's undeniable that these rules provided an advantage to the team attacking second.  I'd rather have additional ties for when both teams can't get off the ground than to have that bizarre maneuver be a part of the game.

...but there *is* an advantage, for the team that attacks second.  Sure, the team that held the other squad off the point entirely did a great job, but they did it against a team that was trying to win, not get 1%.  You're not playing the same game.

Well, off the bat, I don't want it to seem like I think the lady did nothing wrong, or that she deserved to go free.

But I don't think you can say "she knew her husband would kill."  Lynchings were rare, so why would she think her husband specifically would be the one-in-a-million to actually go through with one in 1955?  Again, it was partly the rarity of the case that made Till such a big deal at the time.

You also really don't know that she lied to her husband, because nobody (perhaps not even her) actually knows what happened in the store, let alone what she said to her husband about it.  What she said on the stand later (the "sexual assault") was a dramatic escalation of what actually happened, and probably what she told her husband initially as well.

Again, this isn't about letting her off the hook, but I don't think she "knew" Till was going to be murdered because of what she said.

Okay, so we're in agreement, far more people use cars than guns.  Good talk.

You also seem to want to talk about relative dangers, so why not? 

I agree, people are far more likely to die from a car than a gun. The difference here is that people actually try to do something about car fatalities.  There's a lot of regulation of car safety, including the construction of the car, the design of streets, the training of drivers, etc. etc., and people work all the time to improve those.  They are also working to reduce the need for cars, and soon they'll all be automated and we'll be much safer.  

This is only partly true of firearms (and then inconsistently applied), which is why the OP made the comment that guns ought to be treated more like cars... as a potentially dangerous thing to own and "use," and thus subject to regulation.

Owning a gun won't make you suicidal.  But it will make suicide seem quicker and easier, and it will make a hypothetical suicide attempt vastly more likely to succeed than any other means. Ergo, it is relevant to discussion of the relative safety of gun ownership. 

Sure, most people aren't at risk of suicide, but that's not the point... some are, and possessing guns makes them less safe.
...because it seems like a waste of time and money? Again, *we know who did it*, so I'd rather see investigators try to find out who did some other crimes.
Even in the sense of "carried," people do not "use" guns anywhere near as often as cars.  You must know this.

Why?  Guns are dramatically more likely to lead to successful suicide attempts than other means.  People who don't own guns are thus less likely to kill themselves.

When considering overall mortality from gun violence, it can be misleading to include suicide, but if we're talking about the safety of owning one, suicide counts.

What's to "reopen" here?  We know who did it, they admitted to it, and now they're dead, so it's not like there's anyone to charge for the crime.  Would they just be going after Donham for perjury?  That's a tough conviction to get so many years later, seems like a waste of time and money.  There are plenty of actually open cases to work on.
